title: From alchemy to chemistry
summary: Learn how alchemy, which did not measure, turned into chemistry, which measures and weighs.
cards.0.p: Alchemy (from Arabic al-kīmiyā) is the ancestor of chemistry. It also existed in China and India. Its Western branch passed from Alexandria to the Islamic world and from there to Europe. In alchemy, real experiments and magic went hand in hand.
cards.0.svg#9: From a dream of change to science
cards.0.once.soru: Alchemists tried to transform substances by heating and mixing them. Which science is this work the ancestor of today?
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: Curiosity about changing matter and lab experiments slowly turned into chemistry.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: Astronomy grew out of watching the sky. Alchemy dealt with matter.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: Alchemy studied how substances change, not living things.
cards.1.p: Alchemists searched for a legendary substance that would turn cheap metals like lead into gold. They called it the philosopher's stone. They tried for centuries, but never made a single gram of gold.
cards.2.p: The other dream was an elixir of life that would cure disease and extend life. It was never found, but the interest in preparing medicines helped pharmacy and medical chemistry grow.
cards.2.once.soru: Alchemists searched for an elixir of life to cure disease. Which profession did this search help develop?
cards.2.once.secenekler.0.neden: Mixing plants and minerals to prepare an elixir slowly fed into pharmacy and medical chemistry.
cards.2.once.secenekler.1.neden: Architecture is about buildings. The search for an elixir led to preparing medicines.
cards.2.once.secenekler.2.neden: The search for an elixir turned toward preparing medicines, not toward the sky.
cards.3.p: Alchemists developed tools such as the furnace, the mortar, the glass flask and the alembic. Jabir ibn Hayyan is credited with making nitric and sulfuric acid, and al-Razi with obtaining alcohol.
cards.3.once.soru: Alchemists could not make gold. So what did they leave to us?
cards.3.once.secenekler.0.neden: Tools like the furnace, mortar, glass flask and alembic, along with their experience in experiments, became the basis of the chemistry lab.
cards.3.once.secenekler.1.neden: No alchemist ever made gold, because no such method exists.
cards.3.once.secenekler.2.neden: They missed their goal, but their experiments and tools passed on to chemistry.
cards.4.p: Heating a liquid and cooling its vapor back into a liquid is called distillation. Substances separate because their boiling points differ. Alchemists developed this method, and today it is used to make perfume and fuel.
cards.4.key: Distillation = evaporate + condense. It separates by boiling point difference.
cards.5.p: In his 1661 book The Sceptical Chymist, Robert Boyle questioned the idea of "four elements". He argued that every claim should be tested by experiment. For Boyle, a substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances is an element.
cards.5.svg#0: Boyle's test: does it break down?
cards.5.svg#9: Element: a substance that cannot be broken into simpler ones
cards.5.key: If a substance breaks down into simpler substances, it is not an element.
cards.6.p: In a closed container the total mass does not change. This is called conservation of mass, and Lavoisier showed it in the 1770s. Burning is a substance combining with oxygen. This ended the idea that a substance called phlogiston leaves things as they burn.
cards.6.svg#0: In a closed container, mass does not change
cards.6.key: In an open container the mass can change. You only see conservation when you weigh everything.
cards.7.h: How did chemistry become a science?
cards.7.p: Alchemists hid what they knew and rarely measured. In chemistry, a claim is tested by experiment, and the result is measured and shared. The cycle of observation, hypothesis, experiment and conclusion is the scientific method.
cards.7.etk.soru: Put each feature where it belongs: alchemy or chemistry as a science?
cards.7.etk.ogeler.3.2: Others could not repeat and check the experiments. This was a flaw of alchemy.
cards.7.etk.ogeler.6.2: Lavoisier's precise weighing is the basis of modern chemistry.
cards.8.p:
• Alchemy searched for ways to transform matter and for the elixir of life, but failed.
• It left behind distillation and lab equipment.
• For Boyle, an element is a substance that cannot be broken into simpler substances.
• Lavoisier showed that mass is conserved in a closed container and that burning is combining with oxygen.
• Experiment and measurement are what made chemistry a science.
quiz.0.q: Match each name or experiment with what it gave to chemistry.
quiz.0.e: Al-Razi is credited with obtaining alcohol. Boyle defined the element by experiment, Lavoisier showed mass is conserved in a closed container, and electrolysis proved that water is a compound.
quiz.1.q: Apply Boyle's definition: put each substance in the right group.
quiz.1.ogeler.0.0: Water: breaks into H₂ and O₂
quiz.1.ogeler.1.0: Oxygen: does not break into anything simpler
quiz.1.ogeler.2.0: Limestone: gives lime and CO₂ when heated
quiz.1.ogeler.3.0: Gold: does not break down in any way
quiz.1.ogeler.4.0: Table salt: gives sodium and chlorine by electrolysis
quiz.1.ogeler.5.0: Sulfur: does not break into anything simpler
quiz.1.e: Water, limestone and salt break down into simpler substances, so they are compounds. Oxygen, gold and sulfur do not break down by any chemical means, so they are elements.
quiz.2.q: Put the steps of the scientific method in order.
quiz.2.e: First you observe something, then you form a hypothesis that explains it. The hypothesis is tested by experiment, and a conclusion is drawn.
quiz.3.q: Acetone boils at 56 °C and water at 100 °C. If you distill an acetone–water mixture, which collects in the receiving flask first?
quiz.3.e: Acetone has the lower boiling point, so it evaporates first, condenses in the cooler and drips into the flask. Distillation separates by boiling point difference.
quiz.3.y.1: Water boils at a higher temperature. The substance with the lower boiling point evaporates first.
quiz.3.y.2: Their boiling points differ, so one evaporates first.
quiz.3.y.3: Distillation is used exactly to separate liquids with different boiling points.
A:baslik: The science of chemistry: from alchemy to chemistry
A:ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Distill a mixture, split water and weigh a closed flask.
A:adimlar.0.metin: The alchemists' biggest goal was to turn lead into gold. Today we know the difference. A lead atom has 82 protons in its nucleus, and a gold atom has 79.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: Why did lead never turn into gold?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: Reactions do not change proton number
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: In a chemical reaction only electrons and bonds change. To turn lead into gold you would have to remove 3 protons from the nucleus. Only a nuclear reaction can do that, and only in tiny amounts.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.yazi: They could not heat it enough
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: A furnace's heat breaks bonds, but it does not reach the nucleus. Even the hottest furnace cannot change the number of protons.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.yazi: They never found the philosopher's stone
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The problem was not a missing ingredient but the type of reaction. No substance can change the number of protons by chemical means.
A:adimlar.1.metin: The flask holds a mixture of water and alcohol. What happens when you heat it?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.soru: When you heat it, which reaches the collecting flask first?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Alcohol boils at about 78 °C and water at 100 °C. So the alcohol evaporates and condenses first. The collected liquid still contains some water, so distillation is repeated to get pure alcohol.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Water boils at 100 °C, so it evaporates later than alcohol.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Their boiling points differ, so one evaporates first.
A:adimlar.2.metin: Since ancient times water was thought to be an element. Is it really? Pass an electric current through water (this experiment was first done in 1800).
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: What happens to the water when the current is on?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: It splits into two different gases
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Hydrogen collects at the negative pole and oxygen at the positive pole. The volume of hydrogen is twice that of oxygen. This is the 2 to 1 ratio in the formula H₂O.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The electric current breaks the water down, and gas collects in the tubes.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: This is decomposition, not evaporation. The gases in the tubes are hydrogen and oxygen, not water vapor.
A:adimlar.3.metin: Robert Boyle proposed a definition in 1661. By this definition, an element is a substance that cannot be broken into simpler substances. Look at what collected in the tubes.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: By this definition, what is water?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Water split into two simpler substances, so it cannot be an element. Water is a compound in which hydrogen and oxygen combine in a fixed ratio.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: That was the old idea, but the experiment showed that water breaks down. In science, the experiment has the last word.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The gases were not dissolved in the water. They separated only through a chemical change, and always in a 2 to 1 ratio. This shows that water is a compound.
A:adimlar.4.metin: You will heat tin in a sealed flask. The tin will slowly turn into a white powder.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.soru: When the heating is done, what does the balance show?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Nothing enters or leaves the sealed flask. The atoms only rearrange, and the total mass stays the same. This is called conservation of mass.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The tin gets heavier, but the oxygen it needs comes from the air inside the flask. The total does not change.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Nothing can escape from a sealed flask, so the mass cannot go down.
A:adimlar.5.metin: Now leave the flask open and repeat the experiment. Watch the balance.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: The mass went up! The tin combined with oxygen from the air. Nothing escaped from the flask. New air came in from outside to replace the oxygen used up.
A:adimlar.6.metin: A chemist says that when a metal burns, phlogiston leaves it, so the metal gets lighter. How would you test this claim with the scientific method?
A:adimlar.6.gorev.soru: Which one really tests the claim?
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: Burn it in a closed container and weigh
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Measurement tests the claim. When tin burned its mass went up, so nothing came out of it. Oxygen went in from the air. This is how the phlogiston idea fell apart.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: In science, evidence counts, not authority. Famous scholars can be wrong too.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Books repeat a claim but do not test it. Testing needs experiment and measurement.
A:kapanis.0: Alchemy searched for gold and the elixir of life, but failed. That is because chemical reactions do not change an element.
A:kapanis.1: Alchemy left behind distillation and lab equipment. Distillation separates by boiling point difference.
A:kapanis.2: For Boyle, an element is a substance that cannot be broken into simpler substances. Water can be broken down, so it is a compound.
A:kapanis.3: Lavoisier showed that in a closed container the total mass before and after a reaction is the same. This is called conservation of mass.
A:kapanis.4: Repeatable experiments and measurement, in other words the scientific method, made chemistry a science.
